components.note: 甘 (sweet) — describes the fruit's taste.
木 (tree) — the sweet fruit of an unspecified tree gave 某 its meaning 'a certain, some.'
禾 (grain/rice plant) — 种 relates to seeds and planting crops.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — 种 is pronounced zhǒng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 他这样做一定有某种原因。
example.pinyin: Tā zhèyàng zuò yídìng yǒu mǒuzhǒng yuányīn.
example.english: He must have some kind of reason for doing this.
example.fact: 某 alone means “a certain, some (unspecified)” and can even be doubled to 某某 for extra vagueness — like English “so-and-so” — while 某种 keeps that same vagueness but locks it onto a category with 种 (“kind, type”), a common hedging device for softening a claim without naming specifics.

components.note: 讠 (speech/writing) — the act of putting words down.
己 (oneself, private) — writing down one's own private notes or memories, giving 记 its meaning 'to record, remember.'
忄 (heart/mind) — 忆 describes holding something in the mind, memory.
乙 (yǐ) gives a sound close to yì, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他还保留着童年的记忆。
example.pinyin: Tā hái bǎoliú zhe tóngnián de jìyì.
example.english: He still holds onto memories from his childhood.
example.fact: In everyday speech “to remember” is almost always 记得 (jìde), not 记忆 — 记忆 functions mainly as the noun “memory,” so using it to mean “I remember...” reads as unusually formal or literary to a native speaker, a common trap for learners translating “memory” and “remember” too literally from their shared English root.

components.note: 乐 is the simplified form of 樂, which depicted a wooden 木 instrument strung with strings 幺, played with a pick 白 — music came to represent joy, giving 乐 its meaning 'happy, music.'
阝 (a mound or place) — 队 pictures people gathering together.
人 (person) — people gathering in one place gave 队 its meaning 'a team' or 'a line/queue.'

example.hanzi: 这个乐队上个月发了新专辑。
example.pinyin: Zhège yuèduì shàng gè yuè fā le xīn zhuānjí.
example.english: This band released a new album last month.
example.fact: 乐 is one of Mandarin's most notorious multi-reading characters: lè (“happy,” as in 快乐) versus yuè (“music,” as in 音乐) — the two readings share no tone relationship at all, and 乐队 always takes the yuè reading since it names a “music team,” never a “happy” one.

components.note: 糸 (silk/thread) — 紧 relates to something pulled taut, as thread is pulled tight when spun, giving its meaning 'tight, tense'
心 (heart/mind) — 急 relates to an anxious or urgent state of mind
刍 (chú) gives a sound distantly related to 急's reading jí, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 遇到紧急情况,请拨打这个电话。
example.pinyin: Yùdào jǐnjí qíngkuàng, qǐng bōdǎ zhège diànhuà.
example.english: In case of an emergency, please call this number.
example.fact: 紧急 almost always modifies a fixed set of nouns rather than standing alone — 紧急情况 (“emergency situation”), 紧急会议 (“emergency meeting”), 紧急出口 (“emergency exit”) — learning it inside these set phrases sticks better than memorizing the adjective by itself.

components.note: 高 depicts a tall tower or palace, with a roof at the top and a base below — a simple picture of height.
A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 我妹妹现在读高中二年级。
example.pinyin: Wǒ mèimei xiànzài dú gāozhōng èr niánjí.
example.english: My little sister is now in the second year of high school.
example.fact: 高中 is short for 高级中学 (“senior/advanced middle school”), sitting above 初中 (junior high, short for 初级中学) in China's three-tier 小学–初中–高中 (elementary–junior–senior) school system — a structure English's single word “high school” doesn't name a junior tier for at all.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — words spoken by a mouth are what reach the ear, giving 听 its meaning 'to listen.'
斤 stands in for the ear in this simplified character — the target that spoken words reach.
口 (mouth) — words spoken by a mouth are what reach the ear, giving 听 its meaning 'to listen.'
斤 stands in for the ear in this simplified character — the target that spoken words reach.

example.hanzi: 你听听这首歌,好不好听?
example.pinyin: Nǐ tīngting zhè shǒu gē, hǎo bù hǎotīng?
example.english: Listen to this song for a sec — does it sound good?
example.fact: Doubling a one-syllable verb like 听→听听 is a common softening device in spoken Mandarin, turning a plain command into a casual, low-commitment suggestion (“just take a listen”) — the same pattern behind 看看 (“take a quick look”) and 试试 (“give it a try”), with the second syllable typically toned down to neutral in speech.

components.note: 一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'
女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.hanzi: 我正好有时间,可以帮你。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zhènghǎo yǒu shíjiān, kěyǐ bāng nǐ.
example.english: I happen to have time right now, I can help you.
example.fact: 正好 sits at the intersection of “precisely” (正, as in 正在) and “good, fitting” (好) — it can describe a lucky coincidence in timing (你来得正好, “you came at just the right moment”) or an exact fit in size or amount, covering ground that English splits across “just in time,” “just right,” and “as it happens.”

components.note: 毛 (hair) — 毫 originally meant a fine, thin hair.

example.hanzi: 他对这件事毫无兴趣。
example.pinyin: Tā duì zhè jiàn shì háowú xìngqù.
example.english: He has absolutely no interest in this matter.
example.fact: 毫 originally meant a fine hair (as in 毫米, “millimeter,” literally a “hair-meter”) — 毫无 borrows that image of the smallest possible sliver to intensify a negation, literally “not even a hair's worth,” the same rhetorical move behind English “not one iota.”

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 提 relates to lifting or carrying something by hand.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 提 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.
酉 (wine jar) — 醒 originally described sobering up from drink, extending to 'to wake up.'
星 (xīng) gives a sound close to xǐng, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 谢谢你提醒我。
example.pinyin: Xièxie nǐ tíxǐng wǒ.
example.english: Thank you for reminding me.
example.fact: 提醒 literally combines “to lift, raise” (提) with “to wake up” (醒) — reminding someone is pictured as “raising them out of sleep,” a vivid compositional image underlying a fairly abstract, everyday verb.

components.note: 方 here depicts a flag or banner, marking a group on the move.
氏 depicts a person following behind — together, a group traveling together, giving 旅 its meaning 'trip, journey.'
彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.hanzi: 我们计划暑假去欧洲旅行。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen jìhuà shǔjià qù Ōuzhōu lǚxíng.
example.english: We're planning to travel to Europe during summer vacation.
example.fact: 旅 is pronounced lǚ with the “ü” vowel — one of a small set of Mandarin syllables (旅, 女, 绿, 吕) that keep the umlaut in pinyin because dropping it (writing plain “lu”) would collide with an entirely different syllable already claimed by “lu” (as in 路, 六); the umlaut is a genuine, load-bearing part of the spelling, not a decorative accent.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 惊 relates to an emotional reaction of shock or fright
京 (jīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 惊's reading jīng
壴 (a drum) — beating a drum in celebration
口 (mouth) — singing along in celebration

example.hanzi: 这真是一个惊喜!
example.pinyin: Zhè zhēnshi yí gè jīngxǐ!
example.english: This is such a nice surprise!
example.fact: 惊喜 fuses “shock, fright” (惊, as in 惊讶) with “joy” (喜, as in 喜欢) into a single word for specifically the pleasant flavor of surprise — Chinese keeps this distinct from a bad shock, which instead pairs 惊 with 吓 (惊吓, “to be frightened”), splitting “surprise” along a good/bad axis that English's one word doesn't mark.

components.note: 手 (hand) — 拿 means to take or hold something in the hand
合 (hé) gives a sound related to 拿's reading ná, from an older, closer pronunciation link
土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.

example.hanzi: 请把你的东西拿走。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ nǐ de dōngxi názǒu.
example.english: Please take your things away.
example.fact: 走 tacked onto a verb as a directional complement marks the object moving away from the scene — 拿走 (“take away”) and 带走 (“take/bring along away”) both point outward, while swapping in 来 or 去 instead of 走 would point the same action toward a destination — a small but productive family of verb-plus-direction pairs.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 接 relates to receiving or connecting something by hand.
妾 (qiè) gives a hint of the sound — 接 is pronounced jiē, a connection that has shifted over time.
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 近's meaning 'near, close,' a short distance to walk.
斤 (jīn) gives a sound hint — 近 is pronounced jìn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 他的年龄接近三十岁了。
example.pinyin: Tā de niánlíng jiējìn sānshí suì le.
example.english: He is getting close to thirty years old.
example.fact: 接近 works equally for physical distance (接近终点, “nearing the finish line”) and abstract closeness in age, degree, or time (接近三十岁, “nearing thirty”) — a flexibility English's “approaching” mirrors, while its near-synonym 靠近 is used mainly for the physical sense.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 逮 describes chasing and catching someone.
隶 (lì) gives a sound distantly related to 逮's reading dǎi, having drifted apart over time.
扌 (hand) — 捕 describes catching something with the hands.
甫 (fǔ) gives a sound close to bǔ, sharing the same kind of initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 警方逮捕了三名嫌疑人。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng dàibǔ le sān míng xiányírén.
example.english: The police arrested three suspects.
example.fact: 逮 carries two different readings depending on register — the colloquial dǎi (“to catch, nab,” as in 猫逮老鼠, “the cat catches mice”) versus the formal, legal dài used only in 逮捕 (“to arrest”) — the same character splits into an everyday reading and a bureaucratic one, and mixing them up is an easy slip for learners.

components.note: 立 (to stand) — 旁 relates to standing to the side of something.
方 (fāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 旁.
辶 (walking/movement) — links 边's meaning to a boundary or edge one moves along.
臱 (biān) gives the sound — 边 is also pronounced biān, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 银行就在超市旁边。
example.pinyin: Yínháng jiù zài chāoshì pángbiān.
example.english: The bank is right next to the supermarket.
example.fact: 旁边 is one of Mandarin's location nouns: it attaches directly after the noun it modifies (超市旁边, “next to the supermarket”) and then combines with 在 to form a place phrase — unlike English “next to,” which acts as a preposition, 旁边 grammatically behaves as a noun meaning “the side/vicinity,” a structural quirk it shares with 里面 (“inside”) and 上面 (“on top”).

components.note: 氵 (water) — 激 originally described water dashing or surging forcefully
敫 (jiǎo) gives a sound distantly related to 激's reading jī, having drifted apart over time
力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,他非常激动。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā fēicháng jīdòng.
example.english: Hearing this news, he became very worked up.
example.fact: 激动 covers a broader emotional range than English “excited” — it can describe the rush of good news, a surge of anger, or being choked up and moved to tears, unified by the sense of being emotionally stirred up rather than a specifically happy thrill, which is closer to what English speakers mean by “excited.”

components.note: 马 (horse) sets the scene — a spirited, high-stepping animal.
乔 (tall, lofty) sits beside it — a horse holding its head high, giving 骄 its meaning 'proud, arrogant.'
亻 (person) — pride and arrogance are human traits.
敖 (áo) gives the sound — a close match for ào, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 父母为她的成绩感到骄傲。
example.pinyin: Fùmǔ wèi tā de chéngjì gǎndào jiāo'ào.
example.english: Her parents feel proud of her grades.
example.fact: 骄傲 can describe either a warm, positive pride (为...骄傲, “proud of...”) or a prickly, negative arrogance (太骄傲, “too arrogant”) depending entirely on context — English keeps these apart as two different words, “proud” and “arrogant,” while Chinese lets one word carry both, leaving tone of voice and context to do the disambiguating.

components.note: Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 他不是老师,而是学生。
example.pinyin: Tā bú shì lǎoshī, érshì xuésheng.
example.english: He isn't a teacher, but rather a student.
example.fact: 而是 never appears alone — it is the fixed second half of the construction “不是...,而是...” (“not X, but rather Y”), used to correct a false assumption about what something is; dropping the 不是 half and saying just “而是” in isolation would sound grammatically incomplete to a native speaker.

components.note: 贝 (shell/money — cowrie shells were historically used as currency) — 员 originally related to counting or officials responsible for accounts, later broadening to mean 'member' or 'personnel.'

example.hanzi: 他是我们团队的重要成员。
example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒmen tuánduì de zhòngyào chéngyuán.
example.english: He is an important member of our team.
example.fact: 员 is Mandarin's general-purpose “person who does/belongs to X” suffix — the same 员 shows up in 演员 (“actor”), 服务员 (“waiter, attendant”), and 教员 (“instructor”) — 成员 simply attaches it to 成 (“to form, to constitute”) for “a person forming part of” a group.

meanings: to keep a close watch over

components.note: 见 (to see) — relates directly to 视's meaning 'to look at, view.'
礻 (a form of 示, shì) gives the sound — 视 is also pronounced shì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这栋大楼一直被监视着。
example.pinyin: Zhè dòng dàlóu yìzhí bèi jiānshì zhe.
example.english: This building has been under surveillance the whole time.
example.fact: 监视 carries a distinctly watchful, often suspicious connotation — closer to English “surveillance” or “keeping tabs on” someone than neutral “watching” — which is why it shows up around security cameras, stakeouts, or parental suspicion, rather than casually watching a movie (that's just plain 看).

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.
忄 (heart/mind) — 性 relates to inner nature or character.
生 (shēng) gives a hint of the sound — 性 is pronounced xìng, a related sound though the initial has shifted.

example.hanzi: 这家公司有很多女性员工。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī yǒu hěn duō nǚxìng yuángōng.
example.english: This company has many female employees.
example.fact: 女性 is the more formal, clinical register for “female” (used in demographics, medicine, official forms), while 女人 is the plain, everyday word for “woman” — much like English distinguishes “female” from “woman” by formality rather than meaning, Chinese draws the same register line between 女性 and 女人.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 权 originally meant a wooden lever or weight, later extended to 'power, authority, right.'
雚 was historically closer to guàn; the pronunciation has since shifted to quán, so the sound link is faint today.
禾 (grain, a growing rice or wheat plant) — 利 pictures a harvest.
刂 (knife) — cutting grain at harvest time was a clear benefit or gain, giving 利 its meaning 'profit' or 'advantage.'

example.hanzi: 每个人都有受教育的权利。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén dōu yǒu shòu jiàoyù de quánlì.
example.english: Everyone has the right to receive an education.
example.fact: 权利 (“a right, an entitlement”) is a common homophone trap alongside 权力 (also quánlì, “power, authority”) — same pronunciation, same tones, a different second character (利 “benefit” vs 力 “force”) and a genuinely different meaning, so context alone has to do the disambiguating in speech.

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
讠 (speech) — 谎 describes false speech, a lie.
荒 (huāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 谎, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 小孩子有时候会说谎。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo háizi yǒu shíhou huì shuōhuǎng.
example.english: Little kids sometimes tell lies.
example.fact: 谎 on its own already means “a lie” (as in 谎言, “a false statement”), so 说谎 is literally “to speak a lie” — a transparent verb-object compound, the same simple building pattern behind 说话 (“to speak words”) and 唱歌 (“to sing a song”).

components.note: 圣 is the simplified form of 聖, which combined an ear (耳, listening) and a mouth (口, speaking) above a standing figure — the image of someone who listens and speaks with special insight, giving 圣 its meaning 'holy, sacred.'
讠 (speech) — 诞 originally described boastful, exaggerated speech.
延 (yán) gives a sound distantly related to dàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 圣诞快乐!
example.pinyin: Shèngdàn kuàilè!
example.english: Merry Christmas!
example.fact: 圣诞 is short for 圣诞节 (“Holy Birth Festival”) — 诞 alone means “birth,” so the word literally names the holiday after a birth, the same 诞 that shows up in 诞生 (“to be born”) and, per this dictionary entry, historically also in the birthdays of other revered figures, including Confucius.

components.note: 黑 pictures a face or window blackened by soot rising from a fire 灬 below — giving 黑 its meaning 'black, dark.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 他是一位来自美国的黑人演员。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi láizì Měiguó de hēirén yǎnyuán.
example.english: He is a black actor from America.
example.fact: 黑人 is built literally from “black” (黑) + “person” (人), paralleling 白人 (“white person”) as Mandarin's basic vocabulary for describing race by skin color — a plainer, more literal naming convention than the more varied and evolving racial terminology English has developed.

components.note: 言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.hanzi: 警方正在调查这起案件。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ ànjiàn.
example.english: The police are investigating this case.
example.fact: 警方 refers to “the police” as an institution or authority (as in news reports: 警方表示..., “police stated that...”), while 警察 names the individual officers themselves — similar to English “police” (the force) versus “a police officer” (a person), except Chinese marks the distinction with two entirely different words rather than one word doing double duty.

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'
囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.

example.hanzi: 他明年要去法国留学。
example.pinyin: Tā míngnián yào qù Fǎguó liúxué.
example.english: He's going to France next year to study abroad.
example.fact: 法 in 法国 is a phonetic borrowing, not a meaning-based translation — it approximates the sound of “France” (from the older, fuller transliteration 法兰西, Fǎlánxī), the same strategy behind 美国 (“America,” from 亚美利加) and 德国 (“Germany,” from 德意志) — most country names in Chinese are built this way, sound-first, then shortened to one syllable plus 国 (“country”).

components.note: 钅 (metal/gold) — represents something valuable.
昔 (formerly, in the past) — valuable metal that has been mishandled or lost over time gave 错 its meaning 'mistake, wrong.'
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.hanzi: 我们差点错过了火车。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen chàdiǎn cuòguò le huǒchē.
example.english: We almost missed the train.
example.fact: 错过 combines “mistake, wrong” (错) with the directional complement 过 (“to pass, go past”) — literally “to wrongly pass by” — the same 过 that turns a plain verb into “go past it” shows up in 走过 (“to walk past”) and 路过 (“to pass by”).

components.note: 言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
口 (mouth) — the act of speaking.
牛 (ox) — traditionally read as speaking with the forceful weight of an ox, giving 告 its meaning 'to tell, announce, inform.'

example.hanzi: 老师警告他不要再迟到。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī jǐnggào tā búyào zài chídào.
example.english: The teacher warned him not to be late again.
example.fact: 警告 sits alongside 告诉 as two of several everyday compounds built on the root 告 (“to inform, announce”) — 警告 adds 警 (“alert, alarm”) to sharpen 告 into a formal caution, distinct from the neutral information-sharing of plain 告诉.

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.hanzi: 老天,这也太巧了吧!
example.pinyin: Lǎotiān, zhè yě tài qiǎo le ba!
example.english: Good heavens, what a coincidence!
example.fact: 老天 is a casual, spoken stand-in for “Heaven” as an impersonal, fate-controlling force rather than any specific deity — closer in flavor to English “Good God!” or “Heavens!” as an exclamation of surprise than to a formal religious reference; the solemn, formal term for the cosmic Heaven is simply 天, and adding 老 (here an informal, affectionate prefix, as in 老朋友) tips the register toward the colloquial.

components.note: 酉 (a wine jar) — the vessel holding the drink
氵 (liquid) — the wine itself inside the jar
广 (shelter/building) — 店 names a building used for business.
占 (zhàn) gives a sound distantly related to diàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 我们订了市中心的一家酒店。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen dìng le shìzhōngxīn de yì jiā jiǔdiàn.
example.english: We booked a hotel in the city center.
example.fact: 酒店 literally means “wine shop” (酒 “alcohol” + 店 “shop”) and once named exactly that, but in modern Mainland usage it has drifted to mean primarily “hotel” — a word whose original, dictionary-first sense has been almost entirely displaced by a newer, now-dominant one in everyday speech, while Taiwan usage keeps a “hostess club” sense alive as yet another branch of the same drift.

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.

example.hanzi: 他喜欢苹果、香蕉之类的水果。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan píngguǒ, xiāngjiāo zhīlèi de shuǐguǒ.
example.english: He likes fruits like apples, bananas, and so on.
example.fact: 之类 always closes out a list with 的 attached (“...之类的”), functioning much like English “etc.” or “and so on,” but grammatically it patches onto the last item as though it were itself modifying the following noun — a structural pattern (“A、B之类的C”) with no single-word English equivalent.

components.note: 冖 (a covering shape) at the top represents headwear.
元 (a person, here the head or top part of a person) in the middle is who wears it.
寸 (a hand) at the bottom shows the act of putting it on, giving 冠 its meaning 'crown, cap.'
冖 here is a distorted form of 力 (strength) — a simplified way of showing soldiers grouped together.
车 (cart/vehicle) — 军 originally pictured soldiers riding out to battle in war chariots.

example.hanzi: 她赢得了这次比赛的冠军。
example.pinyin: Tā yíngdé le zhè cì bǐsài de guànjūn.
example.english: She won the championship in this competition.
example.fact: 冠 by itself means “crown, cap” (pictured by its components 冖, headwear, over 元, a head, with 寸, a hand, putting it on) — 冠军 traditionally named the foremost, “crowned” unit or commander in an army, a martial origin that has since broadened from armies to any competition's top finisher.

meanings: to try (to see what it's like or whether one can do it)

components.note: 云 here stands in for an older form meaning "to speak of, to taste," 尝's core meaning.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound distantly related to cháng, having drifted apart over time.
讠 (speech) — 试 relates to proposing or trying something out
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 试's pronunciation shì

example.hanzi: 他决定尝试一种新的学习方法。
example.pinyin: Tā juédìng chángshì yì zhǒng xīn de xuéxí fāngfǎ.
example.english: He decided to try a new way of studying.
example.fact: 尝 alone already means “to taste” (as in 尝一尝, “have a taste”) — 尝试 extends that literal sense of testing something by taste into the abstract idea of “trying” any new method or experience, a metaphor from mouth to mind that English's “try” (from Old French, “to sift, select”) arrived at along a completely different route.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with a stick) — 教 relates to instructing or disciplining, the traditional action of teaching.
孝 (xiào) gives a hint of the sound — 教 is pronounced jiào, a connection that has shifted somewhat.
纟 (thread) — 练 originally meant to boil and whiten silk thread, extending to 'to practice, to train' through repeated refinement.
柬 (jiǎn) gives a sound distantly related to liàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 我们的篮球教练很严格。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de lánqiú jiàoliàn hěn yángé.
example.english: Our basketball coach is very strict.
example.fact: 练 alone means “to practice, to train” (as in 练习, “to practice”), and adding 教 (“to teach”) gives 教练 both a verb sense (“to coach”) and, more commonly today, a noun sense (“a coach/trainer”) — most often heard as a job title shouted across a sports field rather than used as a verb.

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.hanzi: 我不知道对方是谁。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bù zhīdào duìfāng shì shéi.
example.english: I don't know who the other person is.
example.fact: 对方 is a relational noun — it only means anything in reference to “this side” of an interaction (a conversation, a deal, a match), never naming a person the way a name or “he/she” would; English's closest match, “the other party,” carries the same built-in relational logic but sounds notably more formal or legal than 对方 does in everyday Mandarin.

components.note: 阝 (a mound/city) — represents a place being traveled to.
迶 depicts walking or moving along a path — following someone to the city gave 随 its meaning 'to follow, along with.'
日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.hanzi: 有问题可以随时联系我。
example.pinyin: Yǒu wèntí kěyǐ suíshí liánxì wǒ.
example.english: If you have questions, you can contact me anytime.
example.fact: 随时 combines 随 (“to follow, to go along with”) with 时 (“time”) — literally “following the time [as it comes]” — an image of flexibility that maps directly onto its everyday meaning “whenever, at any time,” the same 随 that gives 随便 (“whatever, as you like”) its easygoing sense.

components.note: 攵 (to strike) — 敌 relates to conflict and opposition, as with an enemy
啇 (dí) gives a sound close to 敌's reading dí
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 在战争中,他们是敌人。
example.pinyin: Zài zhànzhēng zhōng, tāmen shì dírén.
example.english: In the war, they were enemies.
example.fact: 敌 alone can function as a verb meaning “to rival, to match” (as in 无敌, “unrivaled, invincible” — literally “no rival”), and combining it with the neutral suffix 人 (“person”) grounds that abstract idea of opposition into a concrete noun, “an enemy.”

components.note: Hand — putting things together by hand.
Gives the sound dá, related to dā but drifted apart over time.
Wood — shelves and frames were made of wood.
Gives the sound dāng, related to dàng but drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他们两个是很好的搭档。
example.pinyin: Tāmen liǎng gè shì hěn hǎo de dādàng.
example.english: The two of them are great partners.
example.fact: 搭 alone carries a sense of “to put together, to piece up” (as in 搭配, “to match, pair up”), and 档 relates to a shelf-like frame or slot — together 搭档 pictures two people slotted together to work as a pair, a word most at home describing comedy duos, business partners, or coworkers rather than romantic partners (that's 伴侣 or 对象).

components.note: 人 (person), doubled — one person shown following another depicts the idea of accompanying or coming from somewhere.
Depicts a young wheat or tree branch that has not yet borne fruit — the image of something still incomplete, the source of 未's meaning 'not yet.'

example.hanzi: 我从未见过这么美的风景。
example.pinyin: Wǒ cóngwèi jiànguò zhème měi de fēngjǐng.
example.english: I have never seen such beautiful scenery.
example.fact: 从未 is a more literary, formal register of “never” than the everyday 从来没 — 未 by itself already carries “not yet” in classical/written Chinese (as in 未来, “the future,” literally “not yet come”), so 从未 pairs “from [the start]” with that older negation for a slightly bookish, emphatic “never,” most at home in writing or formal speech.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谈 relates to talking, conversation
炎 (yán) gives a sound close to 谈's reading tán
讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.hanzi: 校长找他谈话了。
example.pinyin: Xiàozhǎng zhǎo tā tánhuà le.
example.english: The principal called him in for a talk.
example.fact: 谈话 carries a more serious or purposeful shade than casual 聊天 (“to chat”) — a 谈话 is more likely to be a formal conversation, an official interview, or a talking-to from someone in authority, while 聊天 is reserved for relaxed, idle chitchat between friends.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 约 originally meant 'to bind, tie up,' extending to 'to agree, arrange' and 'approximately.'
Feather/plume — old writing brushes were made of feathers.
Gives the sound gàn, related to hàn but drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 约翰是我在美国认识的朋友。
example.pinyin: Yuēhàn shì wǒ zài Měiguó rènshi de péngyou.
example.english: John is a friend I met in America.
example.fact: 约翰 is a transliteration built purely for sound, not meaning — 约 (yuē) and 翰 (hàn) were chosen to approximate “John” phonetically, the same strategy behind most foreign personal names rendered into Chinese, where the characters' own literal meanings (“to agree” + “a writing brush”) are just irrelevant background noise.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 许 relates to giving permission through words.
午 (wǔ) gives a hint of the sound — 许 is pronounced xǔ, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.
夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'

example.hanzi: 公园里有许多美丽的花。
example.pinyin: Gōngyuán lǐ yǒu xǔduō měilì de huā.
example.english: There are many beautiful flowers in the park.
example.fact: 许多 sits at a more formal, written-register notch above the everyday 很多 (“a lot of”) — both mean roughly “many,” but 许多 shows up more often in writing or narration, while 很多 is the default choice in casual conversation.

meanings: (genre of traditional Chinese painting) figure painting

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这部小说里的人物都很有趣。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù xiǎoshuō lǐ de rénwù dōu hěn yǒuqù.
example.english: The characters in this novel are all very interesting.
example.fact: 人物 leans toward someone notable or narratively significant — a historical figure, a fictional character, a “personage” — rather than an ordinary, unremarkable person, which is why 大人物 (“VIP, big shot”) feels natural but calling a random stranger on the street 人物 would sound oddly weighty.

components.note: 大 (big) — in 头's simplified form, this element is linked to the idea of 'high' or topmost, since the head sits at the top of the body.
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.hanzi: 他是我们这个小组的头儿。
example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒmen zhège xiǎozǔ de tóur.
example.english: He's the head of our group.
example.fact: 头儿 is a colloquial, spoken-Mandarin word for “boss, leader” — the 儿 here isn't the diminutive “little” sense it carries in words like 女儿 (“daughter”), but rather Beijing-flavored speech's habit of adding a rhotic -r ending to certain nouns, signaling a casual, streetwise register that the plainer, more formal 领导 (“leader”) doesn't carry.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — relates directly to 叫's meaning 'to call out, shout; to be named.'
丩 (jiū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jiào.
亻 (person) — 做 relates to a person carrying out an action.
故 (cause, reason, to happen) — combined with 亻 (person), 做 came to mean 'to make' or 'to do,' someone actively causing something to happen.

example.hanzi: 这种水果叫做火龙果。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng shuǐguǒ jiàozuò huǒlóngguǒ.
example.english: This kind of fruit is called dragon fruit.
example.fact: 叫做 functions almost interchangeably with plain 叫 in most contexts (这个叫什么? “What's this called?”), with 做 adding a slightly more formal, explanatory weight — useful when introducing a term or definition rather than just casually naming something, similar to the difference between English “called” and “known as.”

components.note: 咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'
氵 (water) — 激 originally described water dashing or surging forcefully
敫 (jiǎo) gives a sound distantly related to 激's reading jī, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 我非常感激你的帮助。
example.pinyin: Wǒ fēicháng gǎnjī nǐ de bāngzhù.
example.english: I'm very grateful for your help.
example.fact: 感激 is a noticeably stronger, more heartfelt “thank you” than the everyday 谢谢 — it names the deep emotional state of gratitude itself (感, “to feel,” + 激, “to be stirred up”) rather than performing the social ritual of thanking, so it shows up in earnest, sometimes formal expressions of appreciation rather than a quick “thanks” in passing.

components.note: A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'
囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.

example.hanzi: 他在中国工作了五年。
example.pinyin: Tā zài Zhōngguó gōngzuò le wǔ nián.
example.english: He worked in China for five years.
example.fact: 中国 literally means “the central/middle country” (中 “middle” + 国 “country”) — reflecting an ancient worldview in which China saw itself as the civilizational center; the same 中 shows up in 中间 (“in between”) and 中午 (“midday”), all sharing that core sense of “the middle.”

components.note: 虫 (a small creature) — 蛋 names an egg, historically grouped together with small creatures like insects and reptiles.
延 (yán) is only distantly related in sound to dàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.
米 (rice) — 糕 names a food made from rice or flour, a cake.
羔 (gāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 糕.

example.hanzi: 生日快乐!我们一起吃蛋糕吧。
example.pinyin: Shēngrì kuàilè! Wǒmen yìqǐ chī dàngāo ba.
example.english: Happy birthday! Let's eat cake together.
example.fact: 蛋糕 is a partly borrowed word: 糕 already meant a steamed rice- or flour-based cake in Chinese long before Western-style cakes arrived, while 蛋 (“egg”) was added specifically to mark the egg-rich, Western-style version — a compound that layers a foreign food concept onto a pre-existing native word rather than inventing or transliterating a wholly new term.

components.note: 页 (head) is the semantic root here, though the exact link to 顺's meaning 'to follow' isn't fully clear today.
川 (chuān) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading shùn has diverged.
禾 (grain, a growing rice or wheat plant) — 利 pictures a harvest.
刂 (knife) — cutting grain at harvest time was a clear benefit or gain, giving 利 its meaning 'profit' or 'advantage.'

example.hanzi: 祝你面试顺利!
example.pinyin: Zhù nǐ miànshì shùnlì!
example.english: Wishing you a smooth interview!
example.fact: 顺利 combines 顺 (“to follow along, go with the flow,” as in 顺着河走, “walk along the river”) with 利 (“advantageous, favorable”) — together picturing events flowing smoothly along a favorable current, and it's a fixture of Chinese well-wishing formulas (一路顺利, “safe travels”) in place of a direct “good luck.”
